summary: Describes an experiment in using the DNS to carry routing information, as a possible way to ease the routing table explosion. It defines an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: Instead of every router keeping a huge map, this experiment asks the Internet phone book, DNS, which way to send traffic.

subtitle: Using the Domain Name System to carry routing information.

tldr.problem: Routing tables are exploding as the number of independent networks grows, consuming memory in routers and network bandwidth for routing updates, especially in multihomed stub domains.
tldr.mechanism: DNS RX records (similar to mail's MX records) advertise gateways for a network; routers query DNS to discover which gateway to use for a destination, then use loose source routing to send packets through the gateway.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1383 is an Experimental protocol from 1992 that proposed a directory-based routing scheme. It was not widely deployed; the Internet instead adopted hierarchical addressing (CIDR) and later BGP scalability techniques.

today: RFC 1383 is Experimental and Historic. It was never widely deployed and is not part of the modern Internet routing infrastructure. The Internet resolved routing explosion through CIDR, BGP improvements, and route filtering. Source routing has been largely disabled on the public Internet for security reasons. This RFC remains valuable as a historical perspective on alternative routing architectures considered in the early Internet.

sections.title: The Routing Explosion Problem
sections.content:
In the early 1990s, the Internet faced a routing scaling crisis. The number of independent networks was growing, forcing transit routers to keep increasingly large routing tables. This consumed memory, increased the volume of routing protocol updates (using more bandwidth and slowing convergence), and required every transit provider to implement routing policies for each new multihomed network. The standard solution was hierarchical addressing (CIDR), but this did not easily support customer networks connected to multiple service providers.

RFC 1383 proposes a complementary approach: instead of announcing every network to the global routing tables, keep only one entry (a pointer to a gateway), and use a distributed directory—the DNS—to discover which gateway can reach the destination.
sections.eli5: Keeping maps of millions of networks is expensive. Why not ask a central phone book instead?

sections.title: DNS-Based Routing with RX Records
sections.content:
The scheme generalizes the MX (Mail eXchange) record: an MX record lets mail reach a domain even if it does not accept incoming connections, by listing gateway hosts that relay mail. RFC 1383 proposes RX records (Routing eXchange) to do the same for IP packets. When a domain D with networks is connected via dual-homed gateways I1 and I2, the domain creates DNS RX records that map its networks' addresses to the gateways' Internet addresses, along with a preference value (similar to MX preference). An Internet router trying to reach a host in domain D queries the DNS, retrieves the RX records, and forwards the packet via loose source routing to the preferred gateway, which relays it into the domain.

The key insight is that once a routing decision is made at the source (or at a router near the source), the source-routed packet travels consistently across the Internet to the chosen gateway, avoiding the risk of different intermediate routers choosing different gateways based on incomplete information.
sections.eli5: Put the network's gateway address in DNS. When a router needs to reach the network, it asks DNS, finds the gateway, and source-routes the packet there.

sections.title: Challenges and Solutions
sections.content:
Several challenges arose: all intermediate relays would need to access DNS (impractical and expensive), so source-based routing decision-making was required to ensure consistency. Performance concerns about DNS lookups were addressed by analogy to mail routing: if mail (one quarter of Internet traffic) survives DNS lookups for every message, IP routing with caching should also be feasible.

Choosing among multiple gateways required a strategy: list all reachable gateways, prune those known to be unreachable from the local site, and apply preference rules to ensure consistent, redundant paths. Caching query results mitigates repeated DNS lookups. The scheme also required replicated DNS servers in the domain's gateways so that RX records remain accessible even if the domain is temporarily offline.

For the reverse direction (traffic exiting the domain), gateways could relay general routing information so internal hosts see normal routes, or hosts could explicitly source-route packets through a preferred gateway. The return path for ICMP messages required careful handling via reverse source routes to ensure replies reach the original sender.
sections.eli5: Multiple gateways need scores so routers pick consistently. Caching speeds things up. DNS servers in the gateways keep the addresses available.

sections.title: Deployment Incentives
sections.content:
Two motivations for adoption existed: the cooperative spirit of the Internet community (reducing global routing table burden is good for everyone) and economic incentives (service providers could charge customers per announced network number, making the low-cost alternative attractive for multihomed customers).

The experiment was practical to implement: the RFC describes a real Unix kernel-based implementation with a DNS query manager and real-time forwarder. It uses standard TXT records in DNS (not requiring a new record type) and integrates with the IP routing stack by monitoring ICMP unreachable messages to trigger DNS queries.
sections.eli5: Good neighbors reduce the burden on everyone, and providers can charge less for customers who use DNS routing instead of announcing their own networks.

sections.title: The Experiment's Outcome
sections.content:
RFC 1383 was published as an Experimental protocol in 1992 and was never widely deployed. The Internet instead solved routing explosion through classless interdomain routing (CIDR), BGP improvements, and route aggregation. Source routing (used to implement DNS-based routing) fell out of favor due to security concerns (spoofing attacks) and router filtering of source-routed packets. By the 2000s, the Internet had moved decisively toward hierarchical BGP-based routing with MPLS traffic engineering for traffic-engineered paths.

Despite limited adoption, RFC 1383 was prescient: it anticipated many ideas that later appeared in operational routing (like preferential gateways similar to BGP import/export policies, and directory-based path selection similar to segment routing and MPLS Traffic Engineering). The document is Historic, representing a road not taken in the evolution of Internet routing architecture.
sections.eli5: This experiment was clever, but the Internet went a different direction. Today we use CIDR, BGP, and MPLS for routing instead.

left.title: Traditional routing
left.desc: Router has full table of all networks; announces every network.

right.title: DNS-based routing
right.desc: Router queries DNS for gateway; DNS replies with gateway address.
